title: Threat Evasion and Information Propagation in Cognitive Flocks
authors: Priyanka Iyer, Cecilia Soroco, Gerhard Gompper
abstract: Information sharing, threat perception, and collective evasion highlight the advantages of swarm intelligence. Here, we study the behavior of flocks of cognitive agents, based on numerical simulations of the augmented inertial spin model, with an explicit predator. Each agent on the predator-facing side of the flock perceives the threat, triggering collective turns through local interactions. We show that the augmented inertial spin model sustains nearly linear information propagation in the under-damped regime, even with realistic flocking interactions such as local collision avoidance and swarm cohesion in addition to alignment. The turning distance of the flock to a stationary predator scales with the ratio $Δ_p/(v_0\sqrtη)$, identifying an optimal balance between response strength $Δ_p$, flock speed $v_0$, and damping $η$ of information propagation. Fragmentation arises when different parts of the flock turn in different directions, however, fast information propagation can synchronize these responses and maintain flock cohesion while under pursuit. For two predators, a combination of stability analysis and simulations reveals a stark contrast between flock and single-particle reactions, with scattering angle shaped by flock geometry, predator position, and the heterogeneous responses of the detecting front. Together, these results show how information propagation, flock geometry, and dynamics together shapes collective escape, providing general principles relevant to both biological flocks and robotic swarms.
summary: This paper models collective escape in cognitive flocks using an augmented inertial spin model that includes realistic interactions like collision avoidance. It shows that information propagates efficiently, allowing the flock to maintain cohesion while evading a predator. The findings provide general principles linking information dynamics, geometry, and collective survival.
main_problem: The study investigates how information (specifically threat perception) propagates and shapes collective escape behavior in cognitive flocks under realistic physical constraints.
main_result: The model demonstrates that fast information propagation can synchronize responses to maintain flock cohesion during pursuit, and the turning distance scales according to a balance between response strength, flock speed, and damping.
method: The research uses numerical simulations of the augmented inertial spin model, incorporating multiple interaction forces like alignment, collision avoidance, and cohesion.
model_or_system: The system models cognitive agents as active Brownian particles whose dynamics are governed by an augmented inertial spin model, including terms for alignment, local collision avoidance, and cohesion forces.
key_observables: Information propagation speed, turning distance scaling, consensus fraction, and flock splitting probability.
important_parameters: Response strength (Delta_p), flock speed (v_0), damping coefficient (eta), and interaction strengths (K, Omega_a, Omega_f).
main_assumptions: The model assumes point particles and restricts initial threat perception to agents with an unobstructed line of sight to the predator.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate rank curves showing information propagation speed under varying damping coefficients, and turning distance scaling laws derived from varying response strengths and speeds.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the governing equations (ISM with multiple forces) to analyzing information propagation speed, characterizing the scaling of turning distance, and finally contrasting flock vs. single-particle escape dynamics.
why_interesting: While focused on classical active matter, the concepts of non-equilibrium dynamics, collective synchronization, and information flow in complex systems are highly relevant to understanding quantum many-body dynamics and open quantum systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Each vision cone (in two spatial dimensions) is divided into 12 segments, and if a segment contains another particle (shown in black), it is considered blocked (red shading). As a result, the threats (A, B, and C, red) are visible to only a few particles (connected via dashed-lines). The particle at the center of the flock has its entire field of view obstructed and cannot perceive any of the threats.
